\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Mixed Layer Depth Variability in the Subpolar North Atlantic:\\Evidence from a Decade of Argo Profiles}
\author{I.~Sorensen, P.~Okafor, and M.~Lindqvist}
\date{March 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We quantify the seasonal cycle and interannual variability of mixed layer
depth (MLD) in the subpolar North Atlantic using Argo profiles collected
between January 2015 and December 2024. The analysis record was frozen on
2025-11-03 and contains 9{,}812 quality-controlled profiles from 41 floats.
Winter MLDs deepen from about 120~m in the eastern basin to more than
400~m in the Labrador Sea, and the spring restratification date varies by
up to six weeks between years. We show that the leading mode of MLD
variability is tied to the North Atlantic Oscillation, and we provide a
gridded climatology that can be used to evaluate ocean and climate models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
The oceanic mixed layer mediates the exchange of heat, momentum, and gases
between the atmosphere and the ocean interior. Its depth sets the volume
of water that is ventilated each winter and therefore controls the
efficiency of anthropogenic carbon uptake on decadal timescales. In the
subpolar North Atlantic, winter mixing reaches deeper than almost anywhere
else in the world ocean, and the region is responsible for a
disproportionate share of the oceanic uptake of heat and carbon.

Despite this importance, mixed layer depth climatologies disagree
substantially in the subpolar basin. Threshold-based products tend to
underestimate winter MLDs in the presence of compensated temperature and
salinity stratification, while curvature-based products are sensitive to
instrument noise near the surface. The choice of criterion is not a
technical detail: we argue that density-based criteria are \textbf{strongly}
preferable to temperature-only criteria in regions where salinity
stratification is active, because a temperature threshold can misidentify
the base of the mixed layer by more than one hundred metres.

The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is the dominant pattern of
atmospheric variability over the basin and modulates both the heat loss
and the wind stress that drive winter convection. Positive NAO winters
bring stronger westerlies, enhanced heat loss over the Labrador Sea, and
deeper convection, but the spatial fingerprint of this response on MLD
has not been mapped with a homogeneous decade-long record.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we construct a
quality-controlled MLD record for 2015--2024 from Argo profiles using a
hybrid density criterion. Second, we map the seasonal cycle and the
interannual variability of MLD across the subpolar basin and relate the
leading mode to the NAO. Third, we release the gridded product together
with uncertainty estimates for use in model evaluation.

\section{Data}
We use all Argo profiles flagged as good or probably good in the
delayed-mode archive between January 2015 and December 2024 within the
domain $45^\circ$N--$65^\circ$N, $60^\circ$W--$10^\circ$W. After removing
profiles with fewer than ten valid levels in the upper 1000~m, profiles
over topography shallower than 500~m, and profiles flagged for salinity
drift that could not be corrected, the final record contains 9{,}812
profiles from 41 floats. Spatial coverage is densest along the
repeat hydrographic lines and sparsest near the sea-ice edge in winter.

Each profile provides pressure, temperature, and practical salinity at a
vertical resolution of 2~m or better in the upper ocean. Potential density
is computed with the TEOS-10 toolbox. We additionally use the ERA5
reanalysis for surface heat flux and wind stress, and the NAO index from
the Climate Prediction Center, both averaged over the same decade.

For comparison with earlier work we extract the corresponding fields from
two published MLD climatologies. The first uses a fixed temperature
threshold of 0.2~$^\circ$C, and the second uses a fixed density threshold
of 0.03~kg~m$^{-3}$ referenced to the surface. Both products are
interpolated onto our analysis grid for a like-for-like comparison.

\section{Methods}
The MLD of each profile is estimated with a hybrid algorithm that combines
a density threshold with a curvature constraint. We first locate the
shallowest level at which potential density exceeds its 10~m value by
0.03~kg~m$^{-3}$. We then refine the estimate by searching within a
window of $\pm 40$~m for the level of maximum curvature in the density
profile, and we adopt the curvature estimate only when it is shallower
than the threshold estimate and the curvature exceeds a noise-based
significance level. This hybrid choice reduces both the compensation bias
of pure threshold methods and the noise sensitivity of pure curvature
methods.

The processing chain consists of the following steps:
\begin{itemize}
\item delayed-mode quality control and salinity drift correction;
\item vertical interpolation of each profile onto a 5~m grid;
\item MLD estimation with the hybrid algorithm described above;
\item binning and mapping onto a $1^\circ \times 1^\circ$ monthly grid.
\end{itemize}

Monthly gridded fields are produced by objective mapping with a Gaussian
covariance function, a zonal decorrelation scale of 300~km, and a
meridional scale of 200~km. Grid cells with fewer than three profiles in a
month are flagged and excluded from the trend analysis but retained in the
climatological seasonal cycle, where the mapping pools all years.

Trends are estimated by ordinary least squares on the deseasonalised
monthly anomalies, with significance assessed using an effective sample
size that accounts for the lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals. The NAO
regression is computed on the same anomalies after removing the linear
trend, so that the two estimates are independent by construction.

Uncertainty in the gridded fields is quantified with a bootstrap procedure
in which the contributing floats are resampled with replacement two hundred
times. The reported confidence intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th
percentiles of the bootstrap distribution at each grid cell, and they
therefore include both sampling and mapping uncertainty but not the
systematic uncertainty of the MLD criterion itself.

\section{Results}
The climatological March MLD, taken as the peak of the seasonal cycle,
exceeds 400~m in the central Labrador Sea and reaches 350~m in the
southwestern Irminger Sea. In contrast, the eastern basin between the
Rockall Plateau and Iceland rarely deepens beyond 120~m, even in March.
The restratification in spring begins earliest in the eastern basin, with
the median shoaling date in the first week of April, and latest in the
Labrador Sea, where the median date falls in the third week of May.

The interannual variability of winter MLD is dominated by a dipole between
the Labrador Sea and the eastern basin. The leading empirical orthogonal
function of deseasonalised February--April MLD anomalies explains 41\% of
the variance and correlates with the winter NAO index at $r = 0.73$.
During the positive NAO winter of 2020, Labrador Sea MLDs exceeded the
climatology by more than 150~m, while the eastern basin was anomalously
shallow, consistent with the dipole structure.

Linear trends over the decade are modest and spatially heterogeneous.
A significant deepening of about 12~m per decade is found in the
northwestern Irminger Sea, while the eastern basin shows a shallowing of
about 8~m per decade that is not significant at the 95\% level once the
reduced degrees of freedom are accounted for. The 2018 convection event in
the Labrador Sea stands out as the deepest single-winter anomaly in the
record, with mapped MLDs above 600~m in three grid cells.

Compared with the two published climatologies, our product is closer to
the density-threshold product in the interior Labrador Sea but differs
markedly along the slopes, where the temperature-threshold product
overestimates March MLD by 80--120~m. These differences matter for model
evaluation: a model scored against the temperature product would appear
biased deep along the western boundary even when it is unbiased against
density-based estimates.

The mixed layer heat content, computed as the vertically integrated heat
anomaly above the MLD, tracks the NAO regression closely in the Labrador
Sea but not in the eastern basin, where advection by the North Atlantic
Current decouples the heat content from the local forcing. This contrast
reinforces the interpretation of the dipole as a fingerprint of two
distinct physical regimes rather than a single basin-wide response.

\section{Discussion}
The dipole structure of the interannual variability confirms that the
subpolar MLD cannot be characterised by a single basin-wide index, and
that process studies confined to the Labrador Sea risk overgeneralising
their findings. The strong NAO coupling suggests that the predictability
of winter convection is tied to the predictability of the atmospheric
circulation, which remains limited beyond a few weeks.

The carbon implications of these findings are direct. Deeper winter mixing
in positive NAO years exposes a larger volume of the interior to the
atmosphere and increases the ingassing of anthropogenic carbon, while the
compensating shallow anomaly in the eastern basin reduces the exposure of
the thermocline there. Because the two regimes partially cancel in the
basin integral, regionally resolved products such as ours are required to
close the subpolar carbon budget.

\subsection{limitations}
Several limitations should be acknowledged. The float distribution is not
stationary, and the early years of the record have poorer coverage in the
western basin. Our mapping assumes stationary covariance scales, which
smooths the sharpest gradients along the boundary currents. Finally, the
hybrid criterion inherits the uncertainties of the underlying density
measurements, and a small number of profiles with unresolved salinity
spikes may survive the quality control.

\section{Conclusion}
We have presented a decade-long, quality-controlled record of mixed layer
depth in the subpolar North Atlantic based on Argo profiles and a hybrid
density criterion. The record resolves the seasonal cycle, the NAO-driven
interannual variability, and the spatial pattern of trends across the
basin. The gridded product, together with its uncertainty estimates, is
released for use in ocean and climate model evaluation.
Future work will extend the record to the full basin.
We expect the climatology to be particularly useful for assessing the
representation of deep convection in coupled models, and we plan to update
the product annually as new delayed-mode profiles become available.
Future work will extend the record to the full basin.
\end{document}
